metadata.h1: Telecom Site Civil Construction in Aurora, Illinois
metadata.intro: Aurora is where Chicago's financial markets physically live: the CME Globex matching engine runs inside the CyrusOne Aurora I data center on Diehl Road, and CyrusOne broke ground on a second $350 million Aurora campus in late 2024. Illinois' second-largest city (180,542 at the 2020 Census) spreads across four counties — Kane, DuPage, Kendall, and Will — with the Fox River splitting it down the middle and I-88 carrying the corridor's fiber and freight along its north side. CellSite Solutions crews handle the civil scope this market generates: duct bank and hut pads feeding the data center corridor, compound and pad work below the city's 42-inch frost line, and bores under the Fox River, the BNSF racetrack, and the CN belt line at Eola.

designCriteria.asce7Edition: ASCE 7-16 (referenced by the 2021 I-codes currently enforced; Aurora began adopting the 2024 I-code series in 2025 — confirm edition at permit time)

seismic.notes: Northeastern Illinois carries low mapped seismic hazard relative to the southern part of the state (Wabash Valley / New Madrid influence fades north). Publish Ss/S1 only from a USGS design-maps query at the site coordinates; site class is boring-specific.

geotech.dominantGeology: Kane County's surficial geology is Wisconsin Episode glacial material of the Wedron Group — clay-loam diamicton of the Tiskilwa Formation and the Batestown and Yorkville members of the Lemont Formation — with high-level sand-and-gravel terraces flanking the Fox River, formed when a proglacial lake dammed by the Woodstock Moraine overflowed catastrophically. Buried bedrock valleys hold thick Illinois Episode sand-and-gravel fills. Bedrock beneath the eastern county is Silurian dolomite (Joliet, Sugar Run, Racine formations). (ISGS surficial geology of Kane County; ISGS Silurian stratigraphy of northeastern Illinois.)
dominantSoilTypes: Clay-loam glacial diamicton (Tiskilwa and Lemont formations)
Fox River terrace sand and gravel (Henry Formation)

karstRisk.note: Aurora is not in a mapped karst region; drift cover over the Silurian dolomite is generally thick. Solution-widened joints can occur in the dolomite where drift thins, so deep drilled foundations still get screened site-specifically.

geotech.foundationApproachNarrative: The controlling fact on most Aurora sites is glacial cover, not rock: telecom-depth excavations in the Tiskilwa and Lemont diamictons rarely see refusal, so shelter pads and hut foundations are conventionally spread footings and thickened slabs carried below the city's amended 42-inch frost depth. The design question moves horizontally instead — which landform the site sits on. Upland diamicton is firm, low-permeability digging; the sand-and-gravel terraces along the Fox River trench fast but can run wet; and alluvial parcels in the river corridor stack a shallow water table on top of floodplain permitting, in a valley that recorded Illinois' heaviest 24-hour rainfall in July 1996. Tower foundations in the diamicton typically favor drilled piers for uplift and overturning rather than rock sockets. Site-specific borings govern every design; this narrative sets expectations, not parameters.

buildingAHJs.note: Permitting, licensing, and inspections run through the eTRAKiT online portal. Published standing review times are not posted — confirm the current commercial queue by phone when scheduling.

regulatory.wirelessFacilityOrdinanceNote: Small wireless facilities in Aurora are governed by the Illinois Small Wireless Facilities Deployment Act (50 ILCS 840), which caps application fees and sets uniform review shot clocks statewide; the Act is currently scheduled to sunset December 31, 2026 unless extended again. City ROW rules and the public-works contractor license still apply to the civil work.

rowPermitAuthority.name: City of Aurora — Public Works / Engineering (public right-of-way permits)
rowPermitAuthority.note: Any work within the city right-of-way must be performed under a separate Public Works contractor license — the general contractor license issued by Building and Permits does not cover ROW work.

stateDotDistrict.name: IDOT District 1 (Region One — six-county Chicago metro), Schaumburg
stateDotDistrict.note: Utility and access permits on state routes such as US-30, US-34, and IL-56 run through District 1. I-88 itself is the Illinois Tollway's Ronald Reagan Memorial Tollway — a separate authority from IDOT.

oneCallCenter.name: JULIE (Joint Utility Locating Information for Excavators) — Illinois 811
oneCallCenter.note: Notice at least 48 hours (two working days, excluding weekends and holidays) before excavation, statewide and regardless of depth. The Damage Prevention Act was amended effective 2025 — confirm current ticket-life rules on JULIE's law page.

stormwaterAuthority.name: Illinois EPA — NPDES Construction General Permit ILR10
stormwaterAuthority.note: Current ILR10 permit effective September 22, 2023 through August 31, 2028. SWPPP plus NOI before disturbance; IEPA typically processes NOIs within about 30 days. City stormwater permit review under the regional (Kane County framework) ordinance applies separately below the federal trigger.

floodplainAdministrator.name: City of Aurora (NFIP participant; Fox River floodplain mapped in the Kane County Flood Insurance Study)
floodplainAdministrator.note: Floodplain development along the Fox River corridor is reviewed by the city under the countywide flood study; confirm the assigned administrator with Development Services for the specific parcel.

regulatory.permitTimelineNarrative: Sequencing an Aurora telecom site means stacking city layers on top of the state ones. The building permit itself files through eTRAKiT, but before crews touch the right-of-way the company needs Aurora's separate Public Works contractor license — a distinct credential from the general contractor license, with its own bond and insurance file. Compound or route work disturbing an acre triggers the IEPA ILR10 process (SWPPP, NOI, roughly 30-day processing), while smaller disturbances can still catch the city's stormwater review under the Kane County framework. Fox River corridor parcels add floodplain review before anything else moves. None of these queues are published as standing numbers — we confirm each one by phone at scoping rather than promising dates the city hasn't.

electricProviders.name: ComEd (Commonwealth Edison, an Exelon company)
electricProviders.note: New commercial service is requested through ComEd's New Business portal or hotline (866-639-3532); a representative is assigned per project. Published lead times are not posted — schedule energization from ComEd's written commitment, not assumptions.

CyrusOne Aurora II — two-building, 446,000 sq ft campus, groundbreaking October 2024
utilities.longHaulRouteNotes: Because the CME matching engine sits in Aurora rather than downtown Chicago, latency-sensitive fiber and microwave routes from the East Coast financial exchanges terminate here — an unusual concentration of privately built long-haul infrastructure for a suburban market.

postingAuthority.name: Kane County Division of Transportation and the individual road-district townships (Kendall and Will county postings apply on the city's south and east fringes)
postingAuthority.note: Kane County code designates 10-ton limits on specific county highways; township road districts post their own limits seasonally. Check postings on the actual approach route before a shelter or hut haul, not the state map.

seasonalLoadRestrictions.note: State and tollway routes into Aurora are not seasonally posted, so I-88 and the US highways carry heavy loads year-round; the risk is on the last mile of county or township road to greenfield sites.

oversizeOverweightPermitAuthority.name: IDOT — Illinois Transportation Automated Permits (ITAP), state routes only
oversizeOverweightPermitAuthority.note: ITAP covers state-maintained highways only. Illinois law requires separate advance permission from each local jurisdiction and from the Illinois Tollway before moving on their roads — and the natural heavy-haul approach to Aurora, I-88, is a tollway.

logistics.bridgeOrClearanceConstraints: Fox River bridge crossings divide the city's east and west sides; verify the load path for crane and shelter moves across the river rather than assuming the shortest crossing is rated for the load.

railroads.name: BNSF Railway
railroads.crossingPermitNote: Aurora is the western end of BNSF's triple-track Chicago Subdivision (the 'racetrack'), with Eola Yard active on the east side. Wireline and pipeline crossings go through BNSF's national utility-permit process — timelines run long, so crossing applications lead the route schedule.

railroads.name: Canadian National (former Elgin, Joliet & Eastern belt line)
railroads.crossingPermitNote: The ex-EJ&E line crosses the BNSF at Eola on Aurora's east edge; CN handles crossing permits through its own utility process.

railroads.name: Metra (BNSF Line commuter service to the Aurora Transportation Center)

logistics.urbanRowRequirements: ROW work requires Aurora's Public Works contractor license in addition to the permit — with certificate of insurance naming the city as additional insured ($1M general aggregate / $500K per occurrence), statutory workers' compensation, and a $5,000 surety bond on file.

environmental.listedSpeciesNote: Northern long-eared bat (endangered) and Indiana bat are the routine flags for tree clearing in the collar counties; run a project-specific USFWS IPaC query rather than relying on a county list.
environmental.floodplainPrevalenceNote: The Fox River runs directly through downtown Aurora, and the city holds a sobering distinction: the heaviest 24-hour rainfall ever recorded in Illinois — 16.94 inches — fell at the Aurora cooperative gauge on July 17–18, 1996, flooding the Fox and DuPage river systems, killing six people, and causing over $600 million in damage regionally. Floodplain screening on river-corridor parcels is a first-order siting question here, not a formality.

seasonality.narrative: Aurora builds on a classic upper-Midwest calendar read against Chicago-area normals (roughly 38 inches of precipitation and a similar figure in snowfall at O'Hare, 1991–2020, with the normal last spring freeze around April 21): frozen ground December into March, a soft freeze-thaw shoulder in March and April, then a May-through-October production core. What is distinctly local is the summer storm exposure — this is the city that took the state's record 24-hour rainfall in July 1996 — so mid-summer scheduling here treats dewatering capacity and erosion-control maintenance as line items, not contingencies. Verify month-level figures against the NOAA 1991–2020 normals for the nearest station before final publication.

costDrivers.rockNote: Thick Wisconsin Episode drift over Silurian dolomite keeps rock out of telecom-depth excavations on almost all sites; refusal is an anomaly worth investigating, not a budget default.
costDrivers.aggregateHaulNote: Fox Valley sand-and-gravel terraces support nearby aggregate sources, and the dolomite quarry belt of the greater Chicago region is within normal haul range.
costDrivers.readyMixProximityNote: Metro-Chicago ready-mix coverage is dense; plant proximity is rarely the constraint it is in rural markets.
costDrivers.permitFeeNote: Budget the Public Works contractor license, its $5,000 bond, and city permit fees as a distinct line from the building permit itself.
costDrivers.prevailingWageExposure: Two overlapping regimes: the Illinois Prevailing Wage Act (820 ILCS 130) applies to public works for state and local government regardless of funding source, and federal Davis-Bacon attaches to BEAD-funded broadband construction. Municipal fiber work in Aurora — an active possibility given the city-owned network — carries state prevailing wage.
costDrivers.unionJurisdictionNote: Heavy and underground construction in the Chicago collar counties operates in a strongly organized labor market; carrier and public-agency owners commonly expect union-signatory or prevailing-rate crews on this work.
costDrivers.seasonalPremiumNote: December-through-March work prices in frost excavation and concrete protection driven by the 42-inch frost depth; spring township load postings can add routing cost to fringe-area hauls.
costDrivers.narrative: Aurora's civil numbers move on process and season more than on ground. The digging itself is forgiving — deep drift, low rock likelihood, dense ready-mix coverage — so what separates bids is who has priced the city's two-license structure (general contractor plus Public Works for ROW), the tollway and local-jurisdiction permission chain on heavy hauls, prevailing-wage exposure on public and BEAD-funded scopes, and the winter premium below a 42-inch frost line. River-corridor parcels add a genuine floodplain cost layer that upland sites never see. Drivers only — unit pricing comes from borings, the month, and the specific route to the gate.

compliance.stateContractorLicensing: Illinois issues no statewide general contractor license — licensing is municipal. Aurora requires contractors to hold city licenses through the Building and Permits Division, with a separate Public Works contractor license mandatory for any right-of-way work; both require insurance naming the city as additional insured and a $5,000 surety bond. Statewide credentials exist only for roofing (IDFPR) and plumbing (IDPH).
additionalRegistrations: City of Aurora contractor license (Building and Permits Division)
City of Aurora Public Works contractor license (required for ROW work)
compliance.insuranceBondingNorms: Aurora specifies $1,000,000 general aggregate / $500,000 per occurrence with the city as primary, non-contributory additional insured, statutory Illinois workers' compensation, and a $5,000 surety bond.

hazards.designImplications: Two hazard axes shape Aurora site design. Convective: the metro's tornado, hail, and derecho exposure argues for conservative anchorage, generator fuel containment, and equipment tie-downs on every compound. Hydrologic: the Fox River corridor plus the 1996 record-rainfall history make pad elevation, compound drainage, and floodplain screening decisive on river-adjacent parcels. Winter ice and cold set the 42-inch foundation depth and the cold-weather concrete regime. Publish wind and ice loading values only after site-specific ASCE 7 and TIA-222 lookups.

items.headline: CyrusOne broke ground on second Aurora data center campus
items.detail: CyrusOne's $350 million Aurora II campus — two buildings, 446,000 sq ft, 40 MW initial IT capacity — broke ground in October 2024 with a targeted early-2026 opening, joining the Aurora I facility that houses the CME Globex matching engine.

items.headline: Illinois BEAD: $1.04B final proposal still awaiting federal approval
items.detail: The Illinois Office of Broadband submitted its BEAD Final Proposal in September 2025 to connect 156,994 locations with $1.04 billion; as of mid-2026 Illinois was the last state awaiting NTIA approval, with state officials publicly pressing for release of the funds.

items.headline: OnLight Aurora operates the city-owned fiber network
items.detail: Aurora built a municipal fiber ring beginning in 2011 and formed OnLight Aurora to extend the now 137-mile buried backbone to institutions and businesses — an unusual city-owned asset that generates ongoing lateral and extension civil work.

fiber.narrative: Fiber routes through Aurora funnel toward two chokepoints, and both are bores. The Fox River splits the city north to south, so any east-west route crosses it — typically by directional drill, with floodplain review layered on the entry and exit pits. The rail network is the second gate: BNSF's triple-track racetrack ends here at Eola Yard, where the CN's ex-EJ&E belt line crosses it, and both carriers process wireline crossings through slow national permit queues that we file before route engineering is even final. The demand side is unusually deep for a suburb — OnLight Aurora's 137-mile city-owned backbone keeps generating laterals, and the latency-driven private routes serving the CME matching engine terminate on Diehl Road. City ROW work adds Aurora's Public Works contractor license on top of the permit.
localSpecificsReferenced: BNSF Eola Yard / CN ex-EJ&E crossing

primaryScopeIds: small cell and DAS node civil
wireless.narrative: A wireless civil scope in Aurora prices to depth and paperwork before anything else. Every pad and pier goes below the 42-inch frost line the city adopts in its amended Table R301.2(1), which makes December-through-March builds a known premium rather than a surprise. Small-cell and densification work runs under the statewide Small Wireless Facilities Deployment Act (50 ILCS 840) — capped fees, uniform shot clocks — but the pole-base and conduit civil still needs the city's separate Public Works contractor license because it happens in ROW. Densification pressure here is real: Illinois' second-largest city, spread across four counties, with growth pushing into Kendall and Will county fringes where township-posted roads complicate spring shelter hauls. Compound drainage design earns extra attention anywhere near the Fox after what July 1996 demonstrated.
localSpecificsReferenced: Public Works contractor license for ROW

secondaryScopeIds: heavy haul access and crane pads
edge.narrative: Aurora is the rare suburb that anchors a national market: the CME Globex matching engine — the physical point where U.S. futures trade — runs inside CyrusOne's Aurora I data center at 2905 E. Diehl Road, with 184 MW of total power behind it, and CyrusOne broke ground on the $350 million two-building Aurora II campus in October 2024. That gravity pulls exactly our scope: transformer and switchgear pads, campus duct bank, generator yards, and the proximity-hosting enclosures that trading firms keep pushing closer to the engine. ComEd serves the load through its New Business process, and heavy equipment reaches the corridor on I-88 — remembering that the tollway requires its own advance permission for oversize moves, separate from IDOT's ITAP permit.
localSpecificsReferenced: CyrusOne Aurora I / CME Globex matching engine

operations.mobilizationNote: Aurora sits at the far end of one continuous interstate run: I-380 to I-80 east past the Quad Cities, then I-88 — the Ronald Reagan Memorial Tollway — straight into the city, with no seasonal postings anywhere on the through route. That geometry makes Aurora a single-mobilization market where crews arrive the same day they load out and stay over for the duration of a scope. The one route-specific wrinkle is administrative rather than physical: oversize and overweight moves need the Illinois Tollway's own advance permission for the I-88 leg on top of IDOT's ITAP permit, so shelter and equipment hauls get their paperwork stacked before wheels roll. Work programs spanning the city's four counties batch efficiently onto one deployment. Response-time commitments are published only after ops sign-off.

faq.question: How deep do foundations need to go in Aurora, Illinois?
faq.answer: Aurora's amended code table sets a 42-inch frost depth — every shelter pad, pier, and hut foundation we build in the city bears below that line, and winter pours carry protection cost on top of it. We treat the figure as code-cited but still confirm the current ordinance text at permit time, since Aurora was in the middle of adopting the 2024 I-code series in 2025. Site geotechnical work governs the final design.

faq.question: What licenses does a contractor need for right-of-way work in Aurora?
faq.answer: Two separate city credentials: a general contractor license from the Building and Permits Division, plus a distinct Public Works contractor license for anything in the public right-of-way — the general license does not cover ROW work. Both require insurance naming the city additional insured ($1M aggregate / $500K per occurrence) and a $5,000 surety bond, on file before permits issue.

faq.question: How much notice does JULIE require before digging in Aurora?
faq.answer: At least 48 hours, counted as two working days excluding weekends and holidays — Illinois' one-call law applies at any excavation depth. We build the JULIE ticket into every underground schedule and re-confirm ticket-life rules against the current statute, which was amended effective 2025.

faq.question: Which railroads affect fiber routes through Aurora?
faq.answer: BNSF and Canadian National. Aurora is the western end of BNSF's triple-track Chicago Subdivision, with Eola Yard active on the east side, and CN's former EJ&E belt line crosses the BNSF right at Eola — so east-side routes often need two carrier permits within a mile. Both railroads process wireline crossings through national permit queues that run long; we file crossing applications first and design the route schedule around them.

faq.question: Why is there so much data center activity in Aurora specifically?
faq.answer: Because the CME Globex matching engine — where U.S. futures actually execute — lives in the CyrusOne Aurora I facility on Diehl Road, trading-driven infrastructure clusters here rather than downtown. CyrusOne broke ground on a second $350 million Aurora campus in October 2024. For civil work that means ongoing transformer pads, campus duct bank, generator yards, and proximity-hosting enclosure pads along the I-88 corridor.

faq.question: Do small cell projects in Aurora follow city or state rules?
faq.answer: Both layers apply. The Illinois Small Wireless Facilities Deployment Act (50 ILCS 840) preempts much of the local process — capped application fees and uniform review shot clocks statewide, currently scheduled to sunset at the end of 2026 unless extended. The civil side stays local: pole bases, conduit, and restoration in Aurora ROW require the city's Public Works contractor license and permit.

faq.question: When does an Aurora project need a stormwater construction permit?
faq.answer: Disturb an acre — or less as part of a larger common plan — and Illinois EPA's construction general permit ILR10 applies: SWPPP, then an NOI that IEPA typically processes in about 30 days, before ground breaks. The current permit runs through August 2028. City stormwater review under the Kane County framework can apply below that federal threshold, so we screen both at scoping.

faq.question: Is flooding a real siting concern for telecom sites in Aurora?
faq.answer: On river-corridor parcels, yes. The Fox River runs through the middle of the city, and Aurora holds Illinois' 24-hour rainfall record — 16.94 inches on July 17–18, 1996, a storm that flooded the Fox and DuPage systems and caused over $600 million in regional damage. We screen floodplain status before layout on anything near the river and design compound drainage to that history, not to an average year.

faq.question: What does it take to haul a shelter or oversize load into Aurora?
faq.answer: Three permission layers, not one: IDOT's ITAP permit covers state routes only, the Illinois Tollway requires its own advance authorization for the I-88 leg, and each local jurisdiction — city, county, or township — must clear its own roads. In spring, township-posted roads on the Kendall and Will county fringes can force rerouting the last mile, so we verify the full path curb-to-curb before scheduling the haul.

decisionGuidance.heading: Boring versus trenching across Aurora's Fox River corridor
decisionGuidance.body: Every east-west fiber route in Aurora eventually faces the same fork: cross the Fox River and its rail flank by directional drill, or route around them. Our judgment, having priced both: the bore usually wins, but not for the reason people assume. Drilling cost is manageable here — the valley's terrace sands and gravels and the underlying diamicton drill predictably, without the rock-socket premiums of shallow-bedrock markets. What actually decides it is permitting concurrency. A river crossing needs floodplain review; the parallel BNSF and CN corridors at Eola need carrier crossing permits with queues measured in months; an open-cut detour through city streets needs ROW permits under Aurora's Public Works license plus restoration. The bore consolidates the schedule risk into applications you can file early and in parallel — the detour spreads it across a dozen serial approvals, any one of which can stall restoration season. So we file the crossing paperwork the week route options are shortlisted, and we treat frac-out contingency planning in the alluvium as part of the base scope, not an adder. Where a route can ride an existing bridge or city conduit, that changes the math — which is exactly the conversation to have with OnLight Aurora before drawing anything.
